title: You're Running Out of Time
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: Antonius Veritas uses Seneca's On the Shortness of Life and Marcus Aurelius's Meditations to argue that most people squander time because they live as if they were immortal. He catalogs the ordinary ways life leaks away, from resentful evenings to years in unfulfilling work to endlessly postponed apologies, projects, and hard conversations. The essay's central move is to present memento mori not as gloom but as a decision filter: imagining one year left clarifies what to stop tolerating, what to begin, and whom to call. Veritas turns the reflection into a simple Stop, Start, Reconnect exercise so the insight becomes action rather than sentiment. He closes by noting that remembering death also restores savor to ordinary moments, since most last times pass unrecognized while they are happening. The piece ends with a pitch for his Stoa community, but the argument is a self-contained case for disciplined, intentional living.
points: Seneca's claim that life is long enough if used well reframes time scarcity as a problem of squandering rather than of too few years.
Marcus Aurelius's practice of treating his life as already done and everything remaining as extra is offered as a way to cut through procrastination.
A one-year-left thought experiment turns death into a filter for relationships, projects, and resentments that would suddenly look absurd.
The author converts reflection into a Stop, Start, Reconnect audit so memento mori produces concrete behavioral change.
Remembering mortality also heightens appreciation of ordinary experiences, because most last times are not recognized as last while they happen.
quotes: In De Brevitate Vitae, On The Shortness of Life- Seneca begins the essay with a bold accusation. Most of us live as if we’re immortal. We’re under the illusion that we’re entitled to all the time in the world.

We keep postponing reading the book, joining the run club, starting a business, going on that road trip, apologizing to the person we wronged, having that difficult conversation- because we assume we can always do it later.
Seneca thought otherwise. He said life is long enough if we know how to use it well.
Marcus Aurelius had an interesting way to think of this reality. He told himself to think of his life as done and whatever remained as extra.
Imagine you were told that you had one year left. What becomes embarrassing to continue caring about? Who would you call? What would you stop tolerating?

Ask if you’d love to spend one of your final moments with this person before staying in the wrong relationship for another year. Ask how many more mornings you assume the universe owes you before postponing the project again.
Also, other than prompting you into action, thinking of death helps you re-administer taste, enjoyment and value to ordinary life.
And usually, you won’t know it’s the last time while it’s happening. This should change how you participate in your life. You’re not getting another one.
